notes.definition: When an aqueous solution of an ionic compound is electrolysed using inert electrodes, the products depend on the relative reactivity of the elements involved, because water also provides hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions that can be discharged.
explanation: An aqueous solution contains the ions of the dissolved compound and also ions from water. A small number of water molecules break down (ionise) to form hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions: H₂O ⇌ H⁺ + OH⁻. So at each electrode there are two kinds of ion that could be discharged, and only one of them is. Using inert electrodes such as graphite or platinum means the electrodes do not react and the products come only from the solution.

At the negative electrode (cathode), the positive ions present are the metal ions and H⁺ ions. If the metal is more reactive than hydrogen, hydrogen gas is produced. If the metal is less reactive than hydrogen (such as copper or silver), the metal is produced and coats the electrode. For example, sodium chloride solution gives hydrogen at the cathode, but copper sulfate solution gives copper.

At the positive electrode (anode), the negative ions present are the ions from the compound and OH⁻ ions. Oxygen is produced unless the solution contains halide ions (chloride, bromide or iodide), in which case the halogen is produced. So sodium chloride solution gives chlorine at the anode, while solutions of sulfates and nitrates give oxygen, because sulfate and nitrate ions are not discharged.

Examples: copper sulfate solution gives copper and oxygen; sodium chloride solution gives hydrogen and chlorine (leaving sodium hydroxide solution); potassium sulfate solution gives hydrogen and oxygen; copper chloride solution gives copper and chlorine. To predict, deal with each electrode separately using the two rules.

In required practical 3 you investigate what happens when different aqueous solutions are electrolysed using inert electrodes. You develop a hypothesis (for example about which solutions produce a metal at the cathode), set up a cell with carbon electrodes connected to a low-voltage d.c. supply, collect any gases in test tubes over the electrodes and test them. Hydrogen burns with a squeaky pop with a lighted splint, oxygen relights a glowing splint, and chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper white. A pink-brown coating on the cathode shows copper.
keyFacts: Water ionises slightly: H₂O ⇌ H⁺ + OH⁻, so aqueous solutions also contain H⁺ and OH⁻ ions.
Cathode: hydrogen is produced if the metal is more reactive than hydrogen.
Cathode: the metal is produced if it is less reactive than hydrogen (for example copper, silver).
Anode: oxygen is produced unless halide ions are present.
Anode: with halide ions present, the halogen is produced (chlorine, bromine or iodine).
Sulfate and nitrate ions are not discharged; oxygen forms instead.
Test for hydrogen: lighted splint gives a squeaky pop.
Test for oxygen: relights a glowing splint.
Test for chlorine: bleaches damp litmus paper white.
Sodium chloride solution gives hydrogen, chlorine and leaves sodium hydroxide solution.

keyTerms.definition: A solution in which the solvent is water, shown by the state symbol (aq).
An electrode, such as graphite or platinum, that does not react with the electrolyte or the products.
A negative ion formed by a Group 7 element, such as chloride (Cl⁻), bromide (Br⁻) or iodide (I⁻).
OH⁻, a negative ion produced when water ionises; discharged at the anode to form oxygen when no halide is present.
H⁺, a positive ion produced when water ionises; discharged at the cathode to form hydrogen if the metal is more reactive than hydrogen.
A proposal explaining an observation, which can be tested by experiment, for example that metals less reactive than hydrogen will be deposited at the cathode.

workedExamples.title: Predicting products: sodium chloride solution
workedExamples.question: Predict the products at each electrode when sodium chloride solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes.
steps: Ions present: Na⁺ and Cl⁻ from the salt; H⁺ and OH⁻ from water.
Cathode: sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so hydrogen is produced.
Anode: chloride (a halide) ions are present, so chlorine is produced.
Na⁺ and OH⁻ ions remain in solution, forming sodium hydroxide.
workedExamples.answer: Hydrogen at the cathode; chlorine at the anode (sodium hydroxide solution remains).

workedExamples.title: Predicting products: copper sulfate solution
workedExamples.question: Predict the products at each electrode when copper sulfate solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes.
steps: Ions present: Cu²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ from the salt; H⁺ and OH⁻ from water.
Cathode: copper is less reactive than hydrogen, so copper is produced (pink-brown coating).
Anode: there are no halide ions, so oxygen is produced from hydroxide ions.
workedExamples.answer: Copper at the cathode; oxygen at the anode.

workedExamples.title: Predicting products: potassium bromide solution
workedExamples.question: Predict the products when potassium bromide solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes.
steps: Cathode: potassium is more reactive than hydrogen, so hydrogen is produced.
Anode: bromide is a halide ion, so bromine is produced (the solution turns orange-brown near the anode).
workedExamples.answer: Hydrogen at the cathode; bromine at the anode.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the metal is always produced at the cathode, as with molten compounds.
misconceptions.right: In fact in aqueous solution hydrogen is produced at the cathode if the metal is more reactive than hydrogen.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think sulfate ions are discharged to form sulfur or sulfur dioxide.
misconceptions.right: In fact sulfate and nitrate ions are not discharged; hydroxide ions are discharged and oxygen is produced.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the hydrogen and oxygen come from the salt.
misconceptions.right: In fact they come from water, which ionises to give H⁺ and OH⁻ ions.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the test for chlorine is a squeaky pop.
misconceptions.right: In fact chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper white. The squeaky pop is the test for hydrogen.

realWorld: Electrolysis of sodium chloride solution (brine) produces chlorine (for bleach and PVC), hydrogen (a fuel) and sodium hydroxide (for soap and paper).
Copper is purified by electrolysis of copper sulfate solution, and objects are electroplated with metals such as copper or silver using aqueous solutions.
Electrolysis of water with a dissolved salt such as sodium sulfate can produce hydrogen for fuel cells.
higherTier: Half equation at the cathode when hydrogen forms: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂.
Half equation at the anode when oxygen forms: 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻.
Half equations for metals and halogens, for example Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu and 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻.
Reduction (gain of electrons) occurs at the cathode and oxidation (loss of electrons) at the anode.
examTips: Treat the two electrodes separately and give a reason for each prediction.
For the cathode, compare the metal's reactivity with hydrogen; for the anode, look for halide ions.
Learn the gas tests exactly: 'squeaky pop with a lighted splint', 'relights a glowing splint', 'bleaches damp litmus paper'.
In practical questions, mention a low voltage, inert (carbon) electrodes and a well-ventilated room because chlorine is toxic.
Remember the volume of chlorine collected is often less than expected because chlorine is slightly soluble in water.
summary: Aqueous solutions contain H⁺ and OH⁻ ions from water as well as the salt's ions.
Cathode: hydrogen if the metal is more reactive than hydrogen, otherwise the metal.
Anode: oxygen, unless halide ions are present, then the halogen.
CuSO₄(aq): copper and oxygen. NaCl(aq): hydrogen and chlorine.
Required practical 3 uses inert electrodes and tests the gases produced.

questions.question: Copper sulfate solution is electrolysed using inert electrodes. What is produced at the cathode?
markScheme: 1 mark: copper
questions.explanation: Copper is less reactive than hydrogen, so copper ions are discharged and copper coats the cathode. Oxygen forms at the anode, and sulfur is never produced.

questions.question: Which is the test for hydrogen gas?
options: A lighted splint gives a squeaky pop
markScheme: 1 mark: lighted splint gives a squeaky pop
questions.explanation: Hydrogen burns rapidly with a squeaky pop. A glowing splint relighting is the oxygen test, bleaching litmus is the chlorine test and limewater is the carbon dioxide test.

questions.question: Which is the test for chlorine gas?
options: A lighted splint gives a squeaky pop
Damp litmus paper is bleached white
markScheme: 1 mark: damp litmus paper bleached
questions.explanation: Chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper (blue litmus may first turn red). The splint tests are for oxygen and hydrogen, and limewater is for carbon dioxide.

questions.question: Which is the test for oxygen gas?
options: A lighted splint gives a squeaky pop
markScheme: 1 mark: glowing splint relights
questions.explanation: Oxygen supports combustion, so a glowing splint bursts back into flame.

questions.question: Sodium chloride solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes. Which row shows the products?
markScheme: 1 mark: cathode hydrogen, anode chlorine
questions.explanation: Sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so hydrogen forms at the cathode. Chloride ions are halide ions, so chlorine forms at the anode. Sodium would only form from molten sodium chloride.

questions.question: Potassium sulfate solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes. What is produced at the anode?
markScheme: 1 mark: oxygen
questions.explanation: There are no halide ions, so hydroxide ions from water are discharged and oxygen forms. Sulfate ions are not discharged, potassium cannot form in solution, and hydrogen forms at the cathode.

questions.question: Where do the hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions in an aqueous solution come from?
markScheme: 1 mark: water molecules breaking down (ionising)
questions.explanation: A small proportion of water molecules ionise: H₂O ⇌ H⁺ + OH⁻. Inert electrodes do not supply ions.

questions.question: Why is hydrogen, not sodium, produced at the cathode when sodium chloride solution is electrolysed?
options: Sodium is less reactive than hydrogen
Sodium is more reactive than hydrogen
markScheme: 1 mark: sodium is more reactive than hydrogen
questions.explanation: When the metal is more reactive than hydrogen, hydrogen ions are discharged instead. Sodium ions are positive, and sodium is above hydrogen in reactivity, not below.

questions.question: Which aqueous solution would produce a metal at the cathode and a halogen at the anode when electrolysed with inert electrodes?
markScheme: 1 mark: copper chloride
questions.explanation: Copper is less reactive than hydrogen (metal at cathode) and chloride is a halide (chlorine at anode). Sodium bromide gives hydrogen and bromine, copper sulfate gives copper and oxygen, and potassium nitrate gives hydrogen and oxygen.

questions.question: Which half equation shows how oxygen is produced at the anode in the electrolysis of an aqueous solution?
markScheme: 1 mark: 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻
questions.explanation: Four hydroxide ions lose four electrons to give one oxygen molecule and two water molecules. Electrons are lost, so they appear on the right. The other equations are unbalanced or use ions not discharged in solution.

questions.question: Which half equation shows how hydrogen is produced at the cathode?
markScheme: 1 mark: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂
questions.explanation: Two hydrogen ions each gain one electron (reduction) to form one hydrogen molecule. H⁺ + e⁻ → H₂ is not balanced, and the others show electrons lost or the reverse reaction.

questions.question: In required practical 3, why are carbon (graphite) electrodes used?
options: They provide extra ions to the solution
They are inert, so they do not react with the electrolyte or products
markScheme: 1 mark: they are inert / do not react
questions.explanation: Inert electrodes conduct electricity without reacting, so all products come from the solution being tested. They do not add ions or speed up the process.

questions.question: Sodium bromide solution is electrolysed using inert electrodes. Name the product at the anode.
markScheme: 1 mark: bromine
questions.explanation: Bromide is a halide ion, so bromine is produced at the anode instead of oxygen.

questions.question: Predict the products at each electrode when silver nitrate solution is electrolysed using inert electrodes.
markScheme: 1 mark: cathode: silver
1 mark: anode: oxygen
questions.explanation: Silver is less reactive than hydrogen, so silver is deposited at the cathode. Nitrate is not a halide, so hydroxide ions are discharged and oxygen forms at the anode.

questions.question: Describe the test for chlorine gas and give the result.
markScheme: 1 mark: hold damp (blue) litmus paper in the gas
1 mark: it is bleached / turns white
questions.explanation: Chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper. Blue litmus may turn red briefly before turning white.

questions.question: Predict the products at each electrode when magnesium chloride solution is electrolysed using inert electrodes.
markScheme: 1 mark: cathode: hydrogen
1 mark: anode: chlorine
questions.explanation: Magnesium is more reactive than hydrogen, so hydrogen forms at the cathode. Chloride is a halide ion, so chlorine forms at the anode.

questions.question: Explain why copper, and not hydrogen, is produced at the cathode when copper sulfate solution is electrolysed.
acceptedAnswers: copper ions discharged instead of hydrogen ions
markScheme: 1 mark: copper is less reactive than hydrogen
1 mark: so copper ions are discharged (gain electrons) in preference to hydrogen ions
questions.explanation: At the cathode, the less reactive of the metal and hydrogen is produced. Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series.

questions.question: Explain why oxygen is produced at the anode when sodium sulfate solution is electrolysed.
markScheme: 1 mark: the solution contains no halide ions (sulfate ions are not discharged)
1 mark: so hydroxide ions (from water) are discharged, forming oxygen
questions.explanation: Oxygen is produced unless halide ions are present. The hydroxide ions come from the ionisation of water.

questions.question: After sodium chloride solution has been electrolysed for some time, the solution becomes alkaline. Explain why.
acceptedAnswers: sodium ions and hydroxide ions remain
markScheme: 1 mark: H⁺ ions are discharged at the cathode as hydrogen
1 mark: Cl⁻ ions are discharged at the anode as chlorine
1 mark: Na⁺ and OH⁻ ions are left in solution, forming sodium hydroxide (an alkali)
questions.explanation: Removing H⁺ and Cl⁻ leaves the Na⁺ and OH⁻ ions behind. A solution with excess OH⁻ ions is alkaline.

questions.question: In required practical 3, a student electrolyses sodium chloride solution. Equal numbers of molecules of hydrogen and chlorine are produced, but the volume of chlorine collected is smaller than the volume of hydrogen. Suggest why.
markScheme: 1 mark: chlorine is (slightly) soluble in water / dissolves in the solution
1 mark: so some chlorine is not collected as gas
questions.explanation: Chlorine dissolves in, and reacts with, water. Hydrogen is almost insoluble, so nearly all of it is collected.

questions.question: In required practical 3, a student compares the products formed from different salt solutions. State two control variables the student should keep the same.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two: voltage (potential difference); concentration of the solution; time the current flows; type (material) of electrodes; distance between electrodes; volume of solution
questions.explanation: Keeping these the same makes it a fair test, so any difference in products is caused by the salt used.

questions.question: Copper sulfate solution is electrolysed using carbon electrodes. Describe what is seen at the cathode.
markScheme: 1 mark: a pink / brown (copper-coloured) solid coating forms on the cathode
questions.explanation: Copper is deposited on the cathode as a pink-brown layer. No bubbles form at the cathode because hydrogen is not produced.

questions.question: Write the half equation for the reaction at the cathode when copper chloride solution is electrolysed. State whether this is oxidation or reduction.
markScheme: 1 mark: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu
1 mark: reduction (gain of electrons)
questions.explanation: Each copper ion gains two electrons to form a copper atom. Gain of electrons is reduction.

questions.question: Before required practical 3, a student wants to test a hypothesis about which salt solutions produce a metal at the cathode. Suggest a suitable hypothesis and one salt solution that would test it.
acceptedAnswers: metal less reactive than hydrogen deposited
more reactive than hydrogen gives hydrogen
markScheme: 1 mark: a testable hypothesis, for example 'If the metal is less reactive than hydrogen, the metal will be deposited at the cathode; if it is more reactive, hydrogen will form'
1 mark: a suitable solution with a reason, for example copper sulfate (expect copper) or sodium chloride (expect hydrogen)
questions.explanation: A good hypothesis links the product to the reactivity of the metal compared with hydrogen, and can be tested by observing whether a solid or a gas forms at the cathode.

questions.question: Potassium nitrate solution is electrolysed. Name the gas produced at the cathode.
markScheme: 1 mark: hydrogen
questions.explanation: Potassium is more reactive than hydrogen, so hydrogen gas is produced at the cathode.

questions.question:
Describe how a student could investigate the products formed when copper chloride solution and sodium sulfate solution are electrolysed using inert electrodes.
Include the apparatus, how the products would be identified, the expected results and a safety precaution.
markScheme: Indicative content: pour the solution into a beaker (or Petri dish); place two carbon (graphite) electrodes in the solution, not touching; connect to a low-voltage d.c. power supply (about 4 to 6 V); fill test tubes with the solution and invert them over each electrode to collect gases; switch on and observe each electrode; test gases: lighted splint squeaky pop shows hydrogen, glowing splint relights shows oxygen, damp litmus paper bleached shows chlorine; observe any solid on the cathode; expected for copper chloride: copper (pink-brown coating) at cathode, chlorine at anode; expected for sodium sulfate: hydrogen at cathode, oxygen at anode; clean electrodes and keep voltage, time and concentration the same; safety: eye protection; chlorine is toxic so use a well-ventilated room or fume cupboard, low concentration and stop after a short time.

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a clear, logical method with inert electrodes and gas collection, correct tests for at least two gases and correct predicted products for both solutions, plus a relevant safety precaution.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a workable method with at least one correct gas test and some correct expected products.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, for example pass electricity through the solution and test the gas.
0 marks: nothing worthy of credit.
questions.explanation: The method must allow products to be identified at each electrode separately, so gases are collected in separate tubes. Predictions follow the two rules: metal less reactive than hydrogen gives the metal; halide ions give the halogen.

questions.question: Compare the products formed when sodium chloride is electrolysed as a molten compound and as an aqueous solution. Explain the differences.
markScheme: Indicative content: molten sodium chloride contains only Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions; molten gives sodium at the cathode and chlorine at the anode; aqueous solution also contains H⁺ and OH⁻ ions from water; in solution sodium is more reactive than hydrogen so hydrogen is produced at the cathode instead of sodium; chlorine is produced at the anode in both because chloride (halide) ions are present; sodium hydroxide solution is left after electrolysis of the aqueous solution.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): correct products for both, with a clear explanation of the role of water and the reactivity of sodium compared with hydrogen.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some correct products for one or both, with limited explanation.
0 marks: nothing worthy of credit.
questions.explanation: The only difference is at the cathode. With water present, H⁺ ions compete with Na⁺ ions, and because sodium is more reactive, hydrogen is produced. Chloride ions are discharged at the anode in both cases.
